passage: Debates about the informal economy, the vast realm of unregistered firms and unprotected work that employs a majority of workers in many poorer countries, tend to divide into two camps. One sees informality as exclusion. On this account, people sell vegetables on pavements or take casual work on building sites because the formal economy has too few jobs to absorb them; informality is a waiting room, and its occupants would leave if a door opened. The other camp sees informality as a choice. Registering a business, paying taxes and complying with labour law are costly, and for many firms the benefits of formality, such as access to the courts and to bank credit, are not worth the price. Informality, on this account, is a rational response to a state that asks much and offers little.

Each camp marshals real evidence, and each tends to generalise from the cases that suit it. The exclusion view draws on the lives of the poorest informal workers, whose earnings are low, whose hours are long and who report that they would gladly take a salaried job. The choice view draws on a different population: owners of small but established workshops and trading firms who could register, who know what registration would involve and who have decided against it. Both groups are informal. They are not otherwise much alike, and an argument about which of them represents the informal economy is rather like an argument about whether the typical resident of a city is a banker or a street sweeper.

The distinction matters most when governments decide to act. Programmes that cut the cost of registration, by reducing fees, merging permits or allowing firms to register online, are well designed for the second group and largely irrelevant to the first. A woman frying snacks at a bus stand is not informal because the registration form is long; she is informal because what she earns would not cover the obligations that formality brings, and because no employer has offered her anything better. For her, simplification changes nothing. Campaigns that instead treat informality as evasion and respond with fines and evictions fall hardest on precisely those who had the least choice.

It would be wrong to conclude that the informal economy is merely a collection of unrelated cases. The groups are linked, since established informal firms often employ, supply or buy from the poorest workers, and conditions in one tier affect the other. But the links are a reason to design policy for each tier with the others in view, not a reason to pretend that one diagnosis fits all. The question to ask about any informal worker is not whether informality is chosen or imposed in general, but which of the two it is for that worker.

passage: When a person who keeps all her appointments in a phone loses the phone, she often says that she has lost her memory, and the phrase is less of an exaggeration than it sounds. For a growing number of thinkers, the boundary of the mind is not the skin or the skull but the reach of the processes that do a mind's work. If a notebook is consulted as automatically as recollection, trusted as fully and available as readily, then, the argument goes, the information it holds is as much a part of its owner's beliefs as anything stored in the brain. To insist otherwise is, on this view, a mere prejudice in favour of the inside.

The argument has real force, and much of it should be accepted. It is hard to say what principled difference there is between a fact that I must work to recall and a fact that I can retrieve, with less effort, from a list I always carry. Both are stored, both are retrieved, and both guide what I do. Ordinary practice already reflects this: we hold someone responsible for knowing what is written in the diary she relies on, and we speak of a shopping list as remembering things for us. When a skill depends on a tool, as a carpenter's feel for the wood depends on a plane he has used for years, the tool can seem less an object he handles than a part of how he perceives.

Yet the stronger conclusion, that the mind simply is whatever system includes the tool, moves too quickly. Devices differ from memory in a way the argument tends to pass over: they can be edited by other people. A notebook can be altered while its owner sleeps; the contents of a phone can be changed by whoever manages the service on which it depends. Biological memory is fallible, and it too can be distorted by suggestion, but it is not open in the same routine way to the revisions of strangers. The difference is not one of storage but of authority, of who has the standing to change what a person takes to be true.

The better lesson, then, is not that minds are everywhere but that trust has become a part of cognition. Once we lean on external stores, the question of whether our beliefs are sound becomes partly a question about the institutions and people who maintain those stores. That is why the loss, or the quiet alteration, of a device can feel like an injury to the self and not merely an inconvenience. The thesis that the mind extends into its tools is right to notice the injury; it is wrong to think that calling the device a part of the mind explains it.

passage: For much of its short history as a subject of research, the wandering mind was treated as noise. Participants in experiments were supposed to attend to the task in front of them, and the moments when their thoughts drifted to lunch or to an argument with a sibling were lapses to be minimised or averaged away. When researchers began to study these lapses directly, by interrupting people at random moments in their day and asking what they had been thinking about, the first surprise was how common the lapses were. The method had the merit of catching thought in the act, before the thinker had time to tidy it into a more respectable account of where her attention had been. A considerable part of waking thought, it turned out, is about something other than what the thinker is doing.

Two quite different interpretations of this finding have since competed. On the first, mind wandering is a failure of control: it is associated with errors in reading and driving, with poorer performance on tests of sustained attention and, in some studies, with lower reported mood at the moment of wandering. The mind that drifts is the mind that has lost its grip, and the remedy is training in attention. On the second interpretation, these costs are real but partial, and they ignore what the drifting mind is actually doing. Much wandering thought is directed at the future, at plans, rehearsals of conversations and the weighing of unfinished business, and some of the solutions that arrive unbidden in the shower or on a walk may owe something to the same process. On this view the mind that drifts is not idle but working on a different problem, one it has judged, so to speak, more pressing than the task at hand.

Each interpretation, I think, makes the same mistake, which is to speak of mind wandering as though it were one thing with one value. The evidence for costs comes largely from tasks that demand continuous attention, where any lapse is damaging by design, while the evidence for benefits comes largely from situations in which the external task is undemanding, so that little is lost by leaving it. Tasks of the first kind are chosen precisely because they make lapses easy to count, and situations of the second kind because they leave room for thought. It is hardly surprising that the two literatures reach different verdicts, since they are, for the most part, looking at different occasions. Nor does the link with low mood settle the matter. A person who is worried is likely both to feel worse and to find his thoughts pulled towards his worries, so that wandering may be as much a symptom of unhappiness as its cause.

A more useful question is not whether the mind should wander but when, and with what awareness. Drifting during a lecture one has chosen to attend is a cost; drifting while washing dishes may be a free opportunity to think. There also seems to be a real difference between thought that slips away unnoticed and thought that is allowed to roam, as when a person deliberately sets a problem aside and lets her attention go where it will. The second kind is under a loose but genuine control, since the person can notice it and call it back. If this is right, the goal of training attention should not be to abolish wandering, an aim that is probably unachievable and possibly harmful, but to make wandering more visible to the wanderer, so that she can tell which kind of occasion she is in.

passage: For anyone who thinks of natural selection as a relentless editor of waste, the tail of a peacock is an embarrassment, since it is heavy, conspicuous and awkward in flight, and it makes its bearer easier for predators to spot and harder for him to escape. Darwin treated such ornaments as a problem of their own, and proposed that they spread not because they helped their owners survive but because they helped them mate: females preferred them, and the preference was enough to carry the trait forward. That answer, however, raised a second and more awkward question, namely why females should come to prefer an ornament that makes their mates less likely to survive.

One influential reply turns the embarrassment into the explanation. An ornament can work as an honest signal precisely because it is costly. A male in poor condition cannot afford to grow and carry an extravagant tail; only a male with ample reserves, and perhaps with sound inherited qualities, can bear the burden and still thrive. A female who chooses the most lavish display is therefore choosing, without knowing it, the male best able to pay. On this view the cost is not a side effect to be minimised but the very thing that keeps the signal reliable. A cheap signal could be produced by anyone, and a signal that anyone can produce soon carries no information.

The idea has been extended well beyond courtship. Some antelope, on spotting a predator, leap high into the air on stiff legs instead of fleeing at once, which looks like a waste of precious seconds. If the leap advertises that the animal is fit enough to outrun any chase, a predator that heeds it saves itself a fruitless pursuit, and the leaper is spared an attack. Here too, the display persuades because it could not be produced by an animal that lacked the quality it advertises.

It would be a mistake, though, to treat costliness as the whole story. Theoretical work suggests that what matters is not that a signal is expensive in absolute terms but that it is more expensive for weak individuals than for strong ones; a signal equally costly for all would sort no one. Nor need every ornament be honest. Some preferences may persist simply because females who hold them have sons who inherit the admired trait, a self-reinforcing loop that can carry ornaments well beyond any useful information. The costly signal, in short, explains why many displays can be trusted, not why every display exists.

passage: It is tempting to define kitsch as art that is badly made, but this will not do. Many objects that everyone recognises as kitsch are made with considerable skill: the porcelain shepherdess has been painted with a steady hand, the sunset over the lake is rendered with careful attention to the gradations of orange and violet, and the greeting-card verse scans perfectly. Conversely, a great deal of clumsy work, the amateur's lopsided watercolour or the child's drawing of a house, is not kitsch at all. Whatever makes an object kitsch, then, it is not a lack of craft.

A more promising account looks not at the object alone but at the transaction between the object and its viewer. Kitsch offers a feeling that has been decided in advance. The weeping clown, the kitten in a basket, the soldier embracing his mother on a railway platform: each announces the emotion it expects, and the viewer supplies that emotion without needing to look closely at anything. The image functions less as something to be seen than as a switch to be pressed. What is missing is not emotion, of which there is plenty, but resistance: nothing in the work pushes back against the viewer, complicates the feeling, or asks to be noticed for its own sake. A serious painting of grief may also move us to tears, but it usually makes us work for them, by showing grief in a particular face that does not quite match our expectation of what grief looks like.

This account explains why kitsch is so often associated with sentimentality, and also why the association is not quite exact. Sentiment as such is not the problem; a good deal of great art is openly sentimental. The problem is sentiment that has been detached from attention, so that the feeling comes first and the object is merely its occasion. The account also explains why kitsch tends to flatter. Because the emotion it calls up is one we already possess and approve of, tenderness towards the innocent or pride in sacrifice, we come away feeling good not about the work but about ourselves.

None of this requires us to despise those who enjoy kitsch, or to pretend that we never do. A cheap figurine on a grandmother's shelf may carry real memories, and those memories are not made false by the object's lack of ambition. Comfort is a legitimate thing to want from an object. The danger arises only when the habit of ready-made feeling spreads from the mantelpiece to places where attention matters more: to the way we respond to news of distant suffering, say, or to the way public ceremonies ask us to feel about history. There, the switch that kitsch trains us to press can stand in for the harder work of finding out what actually happened.

passage: Arguments about working from home usually turn on a single question: are people as productive at the kitchen table as they are at the office desk? For many experienced professionals the honest answer appears to be yes, or close enough. They know their jobs, they know whom to ask, and they gain hours that once disappeared into commuting. But the question is framed around the output of a worker who is already competent, and it says little about how anyone becomes competent in the first place.

Consider a hypothetical accounting firm that sends everyone home. Its partners notice no fall in billable work during the first year, and the move looks like a clear success. What they cannot see is what their newest recruits are missing. In an office, a junior accountant overhears a senior colleague talking a nervous client through a bad result, watches how a disputed figure is checked, and asks a quick question that would feel too trivial to put in an email. None of this appears in any measure of output, and almost none of it is deliberately taught. It is absorbed, in the way apprentices have always absorbed a trade, by being near people who practise it.

Remote arrangements tend to remove exactly this kind of learning, because it depends on unplanned exposure and remote work is organised around planned contact. A video call is scheduled, has an agenda and ends when the agenda is done. The junior who would have learnt by watching instead learns only what someone remembered to explain. The cost is real but delayed: it shows up years later, as a cohort of mid-career staff who are slower to exercise judgement than their predecessors were at the same stage, by which time the decision that caused it has long been forgotten.

This is not an argument for ordering everyone back to their desks. Offices have never guaranteed this kind of learning; a junior placed among seniors who keep their doors shut learns little more than one at home. Firms can also try to replace accidental exposure with deliberate arrangements, such as pairing juniors with seniors on live work or inviting them to sit in on difficult calls. The point is that such arrangements must be built on purpose, and a firm that judges remote work only by the output of its experienced staff will not notice that it needs them until the damage is done.

passage: Quantum theory is among the most precisely confirmed bodies of physics ever constructed, and it is also, by the admission of many who use it, a theory that does not quite say what it is about. The difficulty is usually called the measurement problem. The theory's central equation describes a system by a mathematical object, the wave function, which evolves smoothly and predictably for as long as nobody looks. Under that evolution a particle can come to be in a combination, or superposition, of possibilities: here and there, spinning one way and the other. Yet whenever an experimenter checks, the apparatus records exactly one result. The textbook rule bridges the gap by decree: at the moment of measurement the wave function 'collapses' to one of the possibilities, with probabilities that the theory supplies.

The trouble is that the rule invokes a notion the theory never defines. A measuring device is made of atoms, and atoms obey the smooth equation; treated as part of the physical system, the device should itself enter a superposition of having recorded each result, rather than recording one. Somewhere between the particle and the experimenter's notebook the smooth evolution is supposed to give way to the abrupt one, but the theory does not say where, or why, or what counts as a measurement in the first place. In practice nothing hangs on the answer, because the boundary can be drawn anywhere convenient without altering the predicted statistics. That is precisely what makes the problem so easy to ignore.

The proposed solutions divide, roughly, by what they are prepared to give up. Some modify the smooth equation, adding a tiny spontaneous tendency to collapse that is negligible for single particles but overwhelming for anything as large as a pointer. Others leave the equation untouched and deny that collapse ever happens: every possible outcome is realised, each in a branch of reality that cannot interact with the others, and the appearance of a single result is simply what being in one branch is like. Still others add a further ingredient to the wave function, definite positions for particles at all times, guided by the wave, so that the outcome was settled all along. A widely discussed physical process, in which a system's entanglement with its surroundings rapidly suppresses the signs of superposition, is often offered as a solution in its own right; it explains why superpositions of large objects are never seen, but on most accounts it does not explain why one outcome occurs rather than another.

Because these rival pictures agree, in nearly every experiment so far performed, with each other and with the textbook rule, a common response is to call the dispute metaphysics, a matter of taste for people who have finished their calculations. The response is understandable but confused. It treats the textbook rule as a neutral baseline from which the interpretations depart, when the rule is itself an interpretation, and an incomplete one, since it relies on a word it cannot define. Nor are the rivals strictly equivalent: the theories that modify the equation predict small departures from standard behaviour in sufficiently large systems, and experiments of increasing delicacy are now searching for them.

None of this obliges the working physicist to choose a side before computing a reaction rate; the theory's practical success is real, and it does not wait on the outcome of the debate. But a theory that works without our knowing what it describes has not thereby been shown to need no description. The measurement problem is not a puzzle from philosophy grafted onto physics. It is a gap in the statement of the physics itself, one that the theory's very success has made easy to step around.

passage: Few findings in happiness research have travelled further than the idea of hedonic adaptation. People who experience a good or bad change in their circumstances, the finding goes, tend over time to drift back towards their earlier level of wellbeing, as though each of us were tethered to a personal set point from which events can pull us only temporarily. In its popular form the idea has hardened into something like a philosophy: since we adapt to everything, the pursuit of better circumstances is futile, and contentment is a matter of temperament rather than of how one lives. The research, read with any care, gives considerably less support to this conclusion than its popularity would suggest.

To begin with, adaptation is uneven. People appear to adjust quite quickly to many gains, such as a higher salary or a larger house, which soon become the new normal against which further comparisons are made. But some conditions resist adaptation stubbornly. Persistent noise, a long and unpredictable commute and chronic pain seem to remain unpleasant year after year, perhaps because they keep demanding attention and never settle into the background of experience. The lesson is not that circumstances do not matter but that they matter selectively: what we stop noticing stops affecting us, and what keeps intruding does not.

A second problem lies in how the evidence is summarised. Many studies report that, on average, a group's wellbeing returns towards its earlier level some time after an event such as marriage or the loss of a job. An average, however, can conceal very different individual paths. A group in which some people end up much happier and others much less happy can show almost no change overall, and the reassuring flat line then describes almost nobody in it. When researchers have examined individuals rather than averages, they have tended to find that a substantial minority do not return to where they began, which is precisely the information that a headline about set points discards.

None of this means that the original insight was mistaken. People do adapt to a great deal, and the observation usefully corrects the belief that one more purchase or promotion will produce lasting delight. The error lies in the step from 'we adapt to much' to 'nothing we do makes a lasting difference'. That step is no more justified than its opposite, and it carries a practical cost, since it can discourage people from changing the very conditions, the noisy flat or the gruelling journey, that are most likely to keep wearing them down.

passage: Few ideas in economics are cited as often, or misunderstood as thoroughly, as comparative advantage. In everyday commentary trade is described as a contest: a country wins when it is better at making things than its rivals and loses when they overtake it. On this view a nation that is less productive than its neighbours in every industry would have nothing to sell and would be wise to close its borders. The principle of comparative advantage was formulated precisely to show why this conclusion does not follow, and the fact that the conclusion is still drawn suggests that the principle is more often invoked than understood.

The core insight concerns opportunity cost rather than absolute ability. Consider a hypothetical lawyer who types faster than any secretary she could hire. It does not follow that she should do her own typing, because every hour spent at the keyboard is an hour withdrawn from legal work that earns far more. The secretary, though slower at typing, gives up much less by doing it. Both are better off when each concentrates on the task in which his or her relative sacrifice is smallest and they exchange the results. The same reasoning applies to countries. What determines the pattern of trade is not which country is best at producing a good, but which country forgoes the least of other goods in producing it, and every country, however unproductive overall, has some activity in which that sacrifice is comparatively low.

Two consequences follow that sit uneasily with the language of contest. First, gains from trade do not require one party to lose: the lawyer and the secretary both gain, and so do a rich and a poor economy that trade on the basis of their differing costs. Second, a country cannot have a comparative advantage in everything, since being relatively better at one activity means, by definition, being relatively worse at another. A government that promises to make its nation competitive in every industry is therefore promising something that is not merely difficult but incoherent.

None of this implies that the critics of open trade have nothing to say. The textbook argument compares two settled states and is silent about the passage between them; workers who lose their jobs when an industry contracts do not costlessly reappear in the industry that expands, and the losses can be concentrated in particular towns for a generation. Comparative advantage can also shift over time as skills and capital accumulate, which is why some economists defend temporary support for new industries. These are serious objections, but they are objections to the timing and distribution of the gains, not to the logic of opportunity cost. They do not restore the image of trade as a race in which one runner's progress is another's defeat.

passage: It has become a commonplace that printing fixed the text. Before the press, the argument goes, every copy of a work was made by hand, and every copyist introduced errors of his own, so that texts drifted further from their originals with each generation of transcription. The press ended the drift: it produced hundreds of identical copies at once, and it was this identity, more than mere abundance, that allowed scholars across a continent to cite the same page and to dispute the same words. The thesis is powerful, and in its broad outline it is not wrong. But it credits the machine with an achievement that took centuries and required far more than machinery.

Look closely at the books of the hand-press period and the identical copies begin to dissolve. Printers corrected errors while a sheet was being run, stopping the press to change a letter or a line and then carrying on; the sheets already printed were too costly to waste and were bound up alongside the corrected ones. Two copies of the same edition may therefore differ on any number of pages, and it is possible that no surviving copy matches any other exactly. Reprints, authorised or not, introduced fresh errors and silent improvements of their own. To a reader of the period, a printed book was a more dependable object than a manuscript, but it was not the guaranteed replica that the commonplace imagines.

What made print seem fixed, then, was less the press than a slowly assembled set of expectations and institutions around it. Legal rights over copies gave publishers a motive to suppress unauthorised versions. Scholarly editors developed procedures for collating copies and establishing a single authoritative text. Readers learned to expect that a citation to page and line would lead others to the same words, and that expectation, once widespread, pressed printers toward the consistency it presupposed. Fixity was in this sense a social achievement that the technology made possible but did not by itself deliver.

The distinction matters because the same commonplace is now being run in reverse. Digital texts, we are told, are inherently unstable: they can be altered silently, updated without notice, made to differ from one reader's screen to the next. That is true of the technology, but the history of print suggests that it is not the whole story. Whether digital texts become stable will depend on whether comparable institutions grow up around them: archives that preserve versions, conventions for citing them, and readers who expect, and demand, that a text once published remains what it was. The machine sets limits; it does not settle the outcome.

passage: Arguments about the cleaning of old paintings tend to repeat themselves with remarkable fidelity. A famous canvas is cleaned; the removal of darkened varnish reveals colours far brighter than anyone living has seen on it; and two parties form at once. One celebrates the recovery of what the painter actually intended, a picture freed from centuries of grime. The other mourns the loss of a mellow harmony that generations had loved, and suspects that the cleaners, in their zeal, have removed not only dirt but the delicate final glazes with which the painter softened his effects.

It is tempting to treat this as a contest between truth and sentiment, with the cleaners on the side of truth. There is something to this. Natural resin varnishes do yellow and darken with age, and a sky that now looks olive may well have been painted as a clear blue; to prefer the olive because one is used to it is to prefer an accident over a decision. Cleaning has repeatedly shown that painters long thought murky were in fact bold colourists, and no honest account of the debate can pretend otherwise.

Yet the cleaners' strongest claim, that they return the painting to its original state, is harder to sustain than it sounds. Pigments themselves change: some blues fade, some greens turn brown, some reds lose their glazes to light long before any restorer arrives. Removing the varnish from such a picture does not take it back to the day it left the studio; it produces a new object, one in which unchanged passages and altered ones sit side by side in proportions the painter never saw. The bright painting revealed by cleaning may therefore be no closer to the original than the dark one it replaced, only differently distant from it.

What follows is not that cleaning should stop, but that it should be described honestly. Every restoration is a judgement about which of a painting's many histories to favour, and judgements can be wrong. The responsible course is to make such judgements in ways that can be undone where possible, to record exactly what has been removed and why, and to abandon the language of revelation in favour of the language of interpretation. A restorer who says 'this is what the painter meant' claims more than any evidence can give; one who says 'this is our best reading, and here is how we reached it' claims only what the craft can support.

passage: Few practices attract scorn as readily as offsetting. A traveller who pays a fee to have trees planted in compensation for the emissions of her flight is compared, almost by reflex, to the sinner who once bought a pardon: she has not stopped doing the harmful thing, the critic says, she has merely paid to feel better about it. A sharper version of the objection imagines a man who wishes to be unfaithful to his wife and pays a friend to remain faithful to his own, so that the total quantity of fidelity in the world is unchanged. If that arrangement is absurd, and it plainly is, why should paying for trees be any different?

The comparison is instructive, but not in the way the critic intends. Infidelity wrongs a particular person, and the wrong consists in what is done to her; another couple's faithfulness does nothing to repair it, because she was never interested in the global supply of fidelity. The harm of greenhouse emissions has an entirely different structure. It does not fall on anyone in particular by virtue of a relationship with the emitter; it arises from the total concentration of gases in the atmosphere, to which every tonne contributes equally regardless of where it came from. A tonne removed in one place cancels a tonne added in another as far as the eventual damage is concerned. Where a harm is aggregate and interchangeable in this way, compensation elsewhere is not a moral sleight of hand. It is, at least in principle, a genuine undoing.

What the fidelity case shows, then, is that offsetting is incoherent for directed wrongs and coherent for aggregate ones. One cannot offset an insult to a colleague by being kind to a stranger, but one can offset a contribution to a shared stock of harm by subtracting an equal amount from it. The serious questions about carbon offsetting are therefore not philosophical but practical: whether the trees would have been planted anyway, whether they will survive long enough to hold the carbon they are credited with, whether the accounts of the scheme can be trusted. An offset that fails these tests is not a pardon; it is simply a fraud, and the right response to it is an audit, not moral disdain.

I do not want to claim that nothing remains of the critic's unease. A person who comes to regard every harm as purchasable may lose the habit of asking whether she should be doing the harmful thing at all, and a culture of easy offsetting may slow the changes in conduct that will ultimately be needed. These are real worries. But they concern the character of the offsetter and the politics of reform, not the question of whether the harm itself has been undone, and they should not be dressed up as proof that offsetting is a confidence trick.

passage: Why do so many religious and quasi-religious groups ask their members to do things that are difficult, uncomfortable or expensive? Long fasts, pre-dawn prayers, restrictive diets, distinctive dress that invites ridicule, vows that forgo income or marriage: from a narrowly economic point of view these look like pure loss. An influential answer, borrowed from the study of animal behaviour, is that the costs are the point. A signal that is cheap to send can be sent by anyone, and so tells an observer little. A signal that is costly to send, and costlier still for someone who does not mean it, is credible precisely because it is hard to fake.

Applied to ritual, the idea runs as follows. Groups that depend on mutual aid, sharing harvests, lending money or protecting one another, are vulnerable to people who take the benefits of membership without bearing its burdens. Demanding rituals screen such people out. Someone who is willing to rise before dawn for years, or to give up foods that everyone else enjoys, is unlikely to be only nominally attached, and the others can extend trust accordingly. The theory also explains a pattern that has often been remarked upon: groups that lower their demands in the hope of attracting members sometimes find that they lose them instead, as the value of belonging falls along with its cost.

This is a genuinely illuminating account, and it captures something that purely symbolic interpretations of ritual tend to miss: that rituals are not only statements of meaning but also transactions with consequences for who can rely on whom, and that their cost is part of how they work rather than an unfortunate by-product. But it is incomplete in at least three ways. First, it explains why a ritual should be costly, not why it should take the particular form it does. Any sufficiently burdensome act would serve as a signal, yet communities care intensely about the precise words, gestures and times of their observances, and would not accept a different hardship of equal cost as a substitute. Second, many of the most demanding practices are imposed on children long before they could choose them. A rite performed on an infant may say something about the commitment of the parents, but it cannot be a signal of the child's own.

The third gap is the most important. The signalling theory treats ritual as a message addressed to observers, as though the performer were already fully committed and merely needed to prove it. Yet people who undertake demanding practices commonly report that the practice changes them: that the fast or the vigil produces the conviction it was supposed to display. If that is so, cost does not only reveal commitment but helps to manufacture it. A person who has sacrificed much for a group has reasons to value it that did not exist before the sacrifice, and the observer who reads his devotion as a signal is reading something that the ritual itself helped to create.

None of these objections overturns the signalling account. They suggest instead that it describes one function among several, the one most visible to an outsider calculating whom to trust. A fuller theory would ask what ritual does to the people who perform it as well as what it tells the people who watch, and would treat the form of a rite as something that matters in its own right rather than as an arbitrary carrier of cost.

passage: It has become a commonplace that the internet would be a more civil place if people had to speak under their own names. The reasoning is simple: a person who cannot be identified bears no cost for cruelty, and a person who bears no cost will be cruel more often. Proposals to require verified identities on public platforms rest on this reasoning, and it has an obvious appeal to anyone who has read the comments beneath a news article.

The reasoning is not wrong so much as incomplete. Anonymity does loosen some restraints; people say things to a faceless audience that they would not say across a table. But the restraint that matters most in face-to-face life is not the fear of being named. It is the expectation of meeting the same people again. A villager who insults a neighbour must live beside her the next day; a commuter who insults a stranger on a train usually need not, and commuters are not famous for their courtesy. What disinhibits is less the absence of a name than the absence of a future in which one's words will have to be lived with.

Seen this way, the relevant distinction online is not between named and anonymous accounts but between identities that are durable and identities that are disposable. A pseudonym used for years in a small forum accumulates a reputation as surely as a name does, and its owner has much to lose by squandering it. Many such forums are known for patient and generous discussion, though few of their members could be identified by an outsider. Conversely, people posting under their real names on large platforms frequently behave badly, perhaps because the audience is so vast and transient that no particular reader's opinion of them seems to count.

None of this shows that identity requirements would do nothing. They might deter some of the worst abuse, and they would make legal remedies easier to pursue. But they carry costs that fall unevenly. The people with most to fear from being named are not usually the trolls; they are the employee describing misconduct at work, the young person asking about a matter their family would punish, the dissenter in a place where dissent is dangerous. A policy that removes their cover in order to inconvenience the cruel has chosen a blunt instrument where a finer one was available: designing spaces in which identities, named or not, persist long enough to matter.

passage: Whenever a much-loved novel reaches the screen, a familiar verdict follows: the book was better. Behind the verdict there usually lies a checklist. Was the heroine's age changed, a subplot dropped, a minor character merged with another, the ending softened? Each departure is counted as a fault, and the best adaptation, on this view, is simply the one that departs least, as though the novel were a fixed list of facts and the film an attempt, more or less competent, to copy that list onto a different surface. The habit is understandable, since readers who love a book feel protective of it, but as a standard for judging films it rests on a confusion about what an adaptation is.

A novel and a film do not tell stories in the same way. A novel can spend twenty pages inside a character's head; a film must find something for the camera to look at. A novel handles time loosely, lingering or summarising as it likes, while a film runs at a pace the viewer cannot slow. To reproduce a book's events faithfully is therefore no guarantee of reproducing what the book does. Imagine a novel narrated by a man whose account of himself the reader slowly learns to distrust. A film that simply stages the events he describes, shot plainly and from the outside, may keep every incident and still lose the book entirely, because the book was never really about the incidents but about the gap between what the narrator says and what the reader comes to see.

Conversely, an adaptation that alters a good deal may be truer to its source. A director who invents a visual device to unsettle our trust in what we are shown, framing scenes so that the viewer begins to doubt them, has understood that novel better than one who preserves its plot to the letter. The right question is not how much was kept but whether the film has found its own means of doing what the book did.

None of this means that every liberty is defensible. Some adaptations borrow a famous title for its prestige and its ready-made audience while discarding everything that made the book worth adapting, and the complaint against them is fair. But it is fair for a different reason than the checklist suggests. Such films fail not because they changed things but because they changed the wrong things, keeping the label and throwing away the substance. Fidelity, properly understood, is a matter of purpose rather than of inventory, and judging it requires the critic to say what a book was for before complaining about what a film has left out.

passage: Any science of consciousness faces an awkward fact at its foundation. The thing it studies is, by most accounts, directly available only to the person who has it, and the scientist learns about it chiefly through what that person says or otherwise signals: I saw the flash, or I did not; the face looked angry; the tone seemed to come from the left. Two opposite attitudes to this fact have been common. One holds that reports are so unreliable, so shaped by expectation, vocabulary and the wish to please, that a science resting on them is no science at all. The other treats a sincere report as the last word, since no one, it is said, is better placed than the subject to know what she experiences.

Neither attitude survives inspection, and the second is the easier to dismiss. People are often wrong about their own experience in ways that can be demonstrated: they confidently describe detail at the edges of their visual field that is not available to them, and they misjudge the order or timing of events they claim to have perceived. A report is a response produced by the subject, shaped by the question asked and the categories available, and it can misdescribe the experience it is about. But the first attitude draws the wrong conclusion from this. Every scientific instrument can misreport what it measures; the usual response is to study its errors, not to throw it away. A report is best treated as evidence about experience, fallible but informative, to be calibrated against other evidence rather than either revered or ignored.

The most productive methods have used reports in exactly this spirit. In masking experiments, the same image is shown on many trials, sometimes followed so quickly by a second image that the first is not reported as seen. Because the physical stimulus is held constant, differences in brain activity between seen and unseen trials can be attributed, at least tentatively, to the difference in experience rather than to the stimulus. The approach is powerful, but it carries a hidden complication. On seen trials the subject not only experiences the image but also prepares and makes a report about it, so some of the activity that distinguishes the two kinds of trial may belong to reporting rather than to experiencing.

To get around this, researchers have designed experiments in which subjects make no report at all, and conscious states are inferred from other signs, such as involuntary eye movements that track which of two competing images is being experienced. Critics point out a circle here: those signs were themselves validated by showing that they agree with reports. If reports are suspect, so, it seems, are the signs that stand in for them. The objection is clever, but it proves less than it appears to. The history of measurement is full of such circles. Early thermometers were checked against the sensation of warmth and then against one another, and in time they came to correct the very sensations against which they had first been checked. A circle of mutual calibration is vicious only if it never widens; when independent methods, each imperfect, are tested against one another and turn out to agree, confidence in all of them can rise together.

None of this guarantees that a science of consciousness will answer every question asked of it, and some philosophers doubt that any amount of correlating brain activity with reports could explain why experience exists at all. That doubt may be justified. But it is a doubt about the reach of the science, not about whether reports can serve as its data, and running the two together has done more to obscure the field than either the sceptics or the enthusiasts have usually admitted.

options.C: show that bodily sensations are a more trustworthy guide to temperature than thermometers are.
options.D: argue that no-report methods should replace reports entirely in the study of conscious experience.

passage: In a handful of democracies, adults who fail to vote without a good excuse are fined a small sum. To many people elsewhere this looks like a contradiction in terms: surely a free citizen is entitled to stay at home. The objection deserves a hearing, but it is less forceful than it first appears. What such laws typically require is attendance, not a vote for anyone in particular. Ballots remain secret, and a citizen who wishes to register indifference or protest can spoil the ballot paper or leave it blank. The duty imposed is closer to that of serving on a jury or completing a census form than to an order about what to believe. A subtler version of the objection holds that deliberate abstention is itself a political statement, a refusal to lend legitimacy to a contest one regards as empty. Yet a citizen who feels this way loses very little under compulsion, since the blank ballot preserves the statement and arguably sharpens it: a deliberately empty ballot can be counted, whereas a deliberate absence is indistinguishable from the absences of those who merely forgot.

The more interesting question is what compulsion actually changes. Where voting is voluntary, turnout is usually lowest among the young, the poor and the recently arrived, so the electorate that politicians court is older and wealthier than the population as a whole. Campaigns respond rationally to this. A large share of their effort goes into persuading their own likely supporters to turn up, and one of the cheapest ways to do that is to make those supporters angry or afraid about the other side. When almost everyone votes, that strategy loses much of its point. There is little to be gained by stirring up people who will vote anyway, and the votes worth competing for belong to citizens who have not yet made up their minds.

Supporters of compulsion sometimes go further and claim that it produces wiser decisions. Here caution is needed. Being required to attend a polling station does not make anyone better informed, and a citizen who resents the obligation may simply mark the first name on the list. Compulsion enlarges the electorate; it does not educate it. Its real contribution is quieter. It shifts the incentives of those who seek votes, away from rousing the faithful and towards addressing the undecided, and it allows the result to claim to speak for nearly everyone rather than for those who happened to feel strongly enough to come out. That is a modest achievement, but in an age of angry campaigning it is not a small one.

options.D: turn up to vote, while leaving them free to spoil the ballot paper or leave it blank.

passage: National accounts were designed to measure what passes through markets, and for most of their history they have counted the meal bought in a restaurant but not the meal cooked at home, the hour a paid nurse spends with an elderly patient but not the hour a daughter spends with her mother. The omission was never a secret: early statisticians acknowledged it and set it aside as a practical matter, since household work was hard to observe and there was no price at which to record it. The result, however, was a picture of the economy in which a large share of the work that keeps people alive appeared to be no work at all.

In recent decades, time-use surveys, in which people record how they spend each part of a day, have made it possible to estimate how many hours households devote to cooking, cleaning and care. Turning those hours into money, however, requires a choice between methods that rest on different assumptions. One method, replacement cost, asks what it would cost to hire someone to do the same tasks. Another, opportunity cost, asks what the person doing the work could have earned in paid employment during those hours. The two methods can produce very different totals, and they can rank the same work differently: an hour of childcare by a surgeon is worth a great deal on the second method and rather little on the first.

Critics sometimes take this disagreement as proof that the whole exercise is arbitrary, but that conclusion is too quick. Every figure in national accounts rests on conventions, and the fact that a convention must be chosen does not make zero, the convention long in use, the neutral one. Recording household care at zero is also a valuation, and almost certainly the least accurate available. Estimates, even rough ones, have changed how policy debates can be conducted: they make it harder to describe cuts to public care services as savings when the work has simply moved into homes.

There is, nonetheless, a limit to what a price can capture. Both methods treat care as a bundle of tasks that could in principle be handed to someone else. Much of it can be. But part of what a family member provides is the fact that it is they who provide it, and that element has no market equivalent because it cannot be bought. A figure for unpaid care is therefore best understood as a floor rather than a measure: it shows that the work is not nothing, without claiming to say what it is worth.

options.B: the number of hours recorded for that task in a national survey of how people use their time.
options.C: the price of the nearest service that can be bought, such as a meal eaten in a restaurant.
options.D: the wage that would have to be paid to someone hired to carry out the same tasks.

passage: When a colony becomes independent, one of the first questions its new government must answer is which language it will govern in. The question is often posed as a choice between authenticity and convenience. On one side stands the language of the former rulers, already established in the courts, the universities and the upper ranks of the civil service, and useful for dealing with the wider world. On the other stand the languages the people actually speak, whose adoption would seem to complete the work of liberation. Put this way, retaining the colonial language looks like a practical compromise with a humiliating past, and abandoning it looks like a costly act of pride.

This framing, however, hides the most important feature of the decision, which is that every option distributes advantage and disadvantage among citizens. In a country where many languages are spoken and none is spoken by a clear majority, choosing one of them as the sole language of administration hands a lasting head start to those who grew up speaking it. Their children will sit examinations in their mother tongue while everyone else's children sit them in a second language. Groups that expect to lose from such an arrangement can be relied upon to resist it, sometimes fiercely, and their resistance is not mere sentiment but a reasonable reading of their interests.

The colonial language has a curious property in this situation: it is equally foreign to almost everyone. Retaining it therefore spares the state from having to declare one community's speech superior to another's, which is one reason several multilingual states have kept it long after they expected to discard it. But equal foreignness is not equal access. The colonial language is already the property of a small educated class, often urban and often wealthy, and keeping it as the language of power entrenches that class's position against the rural majority of every linguistic group. The choice, then, is not between authenticity and convenience but between two kinds of inequality: one that runs between language communities, and one that runs between classes within each of them.

Recognising this does not settle what any particular country should do, and it is not an argument for pretending the dilemma away. It does suggest that the sharpest debates about language after empire have rarely been about nostalgia or national pride, whatever their rhetoric. They have been about who will be able to read the forms, pass the examinations and understand the judge. Policies that use several languages at different levels of government, though cumbersome, are best understood as attempts to spread these costs rather than to escape them.

options.B: its native speakers formed a clear majority in most of the newly independent states.
options.C: doing so spares the state from declaring one community's speech superior to another's.
options.D: it is the language most widely spoken among the rural majority of the population.

passage: Architects tend to speak of a building as finished on the day it is handed over, and most architectural criticism shares the assumption. For its occupants, however, the handover is a beginning. Within a few years the first partitions have gone up or come down, a porch has been enclosed, a garage has become a bedroom, and the building has started to diverge from its drawings. A family grows and then shrinks, a business expands into the floor above, a school changes the way it teaches, and each of these shifts leaves its mark on the fabric. Over a century the divergence can be so complete that little of the original arrangement survives except the outer walls and the structural frame. If we want to know how well a building has been designed, the question of how it absorbs such changes deserves at least as much attention as the question of how it looked when new.

The obvious response is to design for change, and for several decades architects attempted exactly that. Offices and schools were built as open floors with movable partitions, and houses with walls that could slide, fold or be unbolted, so that occupants could rearrange the interior at will. The results were often disappointing. Movable partitions were seldom moved, because moving them was laborious and disturbed the services concealed within them; the flexible plan turned out to be a plan that suited no particular use well; and the occupants, rather than enjoying their freedom, filled the space with improvised screens and cabinets to make the rooms that the design had declined to provide. Designing for every possible use, it emerged, had been a way of designing for none.

The buildings that have in fact proved most adaptable are frequently ones that were never designed with change in mind. Old warehouses and mills, with their regular grids of columns, generous ceiling heights and thick, plain walls, have been turned into flats, studios, schools and offices with surprising ease. Terraced houses built for one family have been divided into apartments and, a generation later, joined up again. What these buildings share is not flexibility in the engineered sense but a kind of slack: dimensions a little larger than any one use required, a structure simple enough to be understood by ordinary builders, and surfaces that can be cut into without catastrophe. The ordinary builder called in to knock two rooms together can see at once where the loads run and what may safely be taken away. They fit their first use loosely, and that looseness is what lets them fit their later uses at all.

The lesson is an uncomfortable one for a profession that prides itself on precision. A building tailored exactly to its brief, every room sized to its programme and every service routed to suit it, is admirable on the day of opening and brittle thereafter, because the brief will change and the building cannot. Generosity of this kind costs something at the outset, in floor area and in height, and clients are seldom eager to pay for space that nobody has yet asked for. This is not an argument against all precision; an operating theatre or a laboratory must fit its use closely, and a little slack in the wrong place is merely waste. But for most ordinary buildings, which will outlive the purposes for which they were commissioned, the more durable virtue is a certain generosity, together with a willingness on the architect's part to regard the occupants' later alterations not as defacement but as the building continuing to do its job.
